items.title: 8.2 Cultural and Ethical Implications of AI Systems

source_refs.note: Topic 8.2 with its Class Activities, Do You Know and Tidbit (PDF 112-115); Fig 8.5 redrawn and the stakeholders carried as a table. Pakistan's regional languages and a note on the 2025 National AI Policy are added; both need review. Short Q5-6 and Long Q2 and Q7 are answered here.

blocks.text: AI affects how people live, work and interact with technology, so its cultural and ethical effects must be considered. AI systems are not only technical creations but social tools that affect individuals, communities and governments (Fig 8.5).

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Debate: should AI make decisions that affect people's lives, such as hiring for jobs or grading students?

blocks.caption: Stakeholders and their concerns
rows: Design and build AI systems, focusing on functionality, innovation and performance; they must make systems accurate, fair and ethical
Use AI systems daily and expect them to be easy and reliable; concerned about privacy, security and correct results
Make policies and regulations for safe, fair use; protect public interests and enforce the law
Experience the impact; focus on preserving social values and cultural norms and promote responsible use

blocks.text: Cultural diversity affects how AI is designed, seen and used around the world. Cultural values shape what users expect about privacy, communication and technology, so designers must consider local traditions and behaviour. Some societies are comfortable sharing data while others demand strict confidentiality; language models must include many languages and dialects (for Pakistan, Urdu and regional languages such as Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto and Balochi) to avoid bias toward dominant cultures; and AI decisions should respect local customs.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: An AI that understands different languages and cultures can serve people from all backgrounds more effectively.

items: Fairness: no discrimination. An admissions AI must not favour or reject students because of gender, region, language or background.
Accountability: someone is responsible. The university must be able to explain who is responsible if the system decides unfairly.
Transparency: decisions can be explained, for example why a student was selected or rejected.
Safety: users are protected from harm. A disease-diagnosis AI must be tested carefully so it does not give harmful or misleading results.

blocks.text: AI learns from large datasets that may hide biases. A hiring system trained mostly on past records in which men were chosen more often than women may unfairly prefer male candidates; a face-recognition system trained mainly on one age group, skin tone or region may work poorly for others. Developers must review and adjust their data, and inclusive design considers diverse perspectives so technology serves everyone equally, regardless of gender, ethnicity or background.

blocks.alt: A central circle labelled AI system is joined to four stakeholder boxes: developers (accurate, fair systems), users (ease, privacy, correct results), governments (laws, public interest) and communities (social and cultural values). A strip below lists the principles fairness (no discrimination), accountability (someone is responsible), transparency (decisions can be explained) and safety (no harm to users).
blocks.caption: Stakeholders and ethical principles in AI (original diagram after Fig 8.5).
blocks.long_description: Ethical design means balancing all four groups, not only the people who build or pay for the system.

blocks.text: Conflicts arise when stakeholders have competing priorities. Businesses want to collect data for innovation and profit, users value privacy and control of their information, and governments must balance economic growth with citizens' rights. For example, a company may gather large amounts of user data to improve its AI, but doing so without clear consent violates privacy and trust; transparent data policies and simple consent options help balance usefulness and ethics.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Balancing privacy and innovation is one of the biggest challenges in today's technology-driven world.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Role-play a company meeting in which developers want to collect user data and privacy advocates oppose it, and discuss solutions.

International frameworks guide responsible AI. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) enforces strict rules on data privacy and user rights, and AI ethics guidelines from organisations worldwide stress accountability, fairness and human dignity. For Pakistan, national AI policies are important to encourage innovation while ensuring ethical compliance: they can regulate data protection, support research and help AI solutions fit local values, building public trust and attracting partnerships.
